claim: PNNs modulated the gain of visual responses in the adult mouse visual cortex in vivo
source: We found that PNNs modulated the gain of visual responses and γ-oscillations in the adult mouse visual cortex in vivo, consistent with increased interneuron function.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in visual response gain following PNN removal, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: PNNs modulated γ-oscillations in the adult mouse visual cortex in vivo
source: We found that PNNs modulated the gain of visual responses and γ-oscillations in the adult mouse visual cortex in vivo, consistent with increased interneuron function.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in γ-oscillations following PNN removal, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 1.

claim: Removal of PNNs in adult V1 did not affect GABAergic neurotransmission from PV cells
source: Removal of PNNs in adult V1 did not affect GABAergic neurotransmission from PV cells, nor neuronal excitability in layer 4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from paired recordings showing no changes in unitary GABAergic transmission, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: Removal of PNNs in adult V1 did not affect neuronal excitability in layer 4
source: Removal of PNNs in adult V1 did not affect GABAergic neurotransmission from PV cells, nor neuronal excitability in layer 4.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing no changes in intrinsic excitability following PNN removal, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: PNN degradation coupled to sensory input potentiated glutamatergic thalamic synapses selectively onto PV cells
source: Importantly, PNN degradation coupled to sensory input potentiated glutamatergic thalamic synapses selectively onto PV cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from optogenetic stimulation experiments showing increased thalamocortical responses in PV cells but not PNs, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 2.

claim: In the absence of PNNs, increased thalamic PV-cell recruitment modulated feed-forward inhibition differently on PV cells and pyramidal neurons
source: In the absence of PNNs, increased thalamic PV-cell recruitment modulated feed-forward inhibition differently on PV cells and pyramidal neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects on feed-forward inhibition onto PV cells versus PNs, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 4.

claim: The effects of PNN degradation depended on visual input, as they were strongly attenuated by monocular deprivation in PNN-depleted adult mice
source: These effects depended on visual input, as they were strongly attenuated by monocular deprivation in PNN-depleted adult mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing effects in control versus monocularly deprived animals, as described in the abstract and demonstrated in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: PNNs control visual processing and plasticity by selectively setting the strength of thalamic recruitment of PV cells
source: Thus, PNNs control visual processing and plasticity by selectively setting the strength of thalamic recruitment of PV cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing selective effects on thalamic inputs to PV cells and their dependence on visual input.

claim: During postnatal maturation, sensory processing goes through a critical period (CP), a developmental interval, in which neural circuits are shaped by sensory experience
source: During postnatal maturation, sensory processing goes through a critical period (CP), a developmental interval, in which neural circuits are shaped by sensory experience.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about critical periods in sensory development.

claim: After the critical period, plasticity declines significantly, and learning becomes more difficult
source: After this time window, plasticity declines significantly, and learning becomes more difficult (Hensch, 2005; Espinosa and Stryker, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on critical period plasticity.

claim: In the visual cortex, the closure of the CP is paralleled by the structural maturation of the extracellular matrix, and, in particular, of perineuronal nets (PNNs)
source: In the visual cortex, the closure of the CP is paralleled by the structural maturation of the extracellular matrix, and, in particular, of perineuronal nets (PNNs).
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about PNN development during critical periods.

claim: PNNs are composed by a conglomeration of chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans, extracellular matrix and cell-adhesion molecules
source: These are composed by a conglomeration of chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans, extracellular matrix and cell-adhesion molecules that, in the neocortex, accumulates selectively around fast-spiking, PV basket cells (Pizzorusso et al., 2002; Berardi et al., 2004; Bernard and Prochiantz, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PNN composition.

claim: In the neocortex, PNNs accumulate selectively around fast-spiking, PV basket cells
source: These are composed by a conglomeration of chondroitin sulphate proteoglycans, extracellular matrix and cell-adhesion molecules that, in the neocortex, accumulates selectively around fast-spiking, PV basket cells (Pizzorusso et al., 2002; Berardi et al., 2004; Bernard and Prochiantz, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research and confirmed by the authors' own immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chemical breakdown of PNNs reactivates ocular dominance plasticity in the adult visual cortex
source: Importantly, chemical breakdown of PNNs reactivates ocular dominance plasticity in the adult visual cortex (Pizzorusso et al., 2002), promotes juvenile forms of extinction of fear memories in the amygdala (Gogolla et al., 2009) and functional recovery after brain injury (Bradbury et al., 2002; Gherardini et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PNN degradation and plasticity.

claim: Chemical breakdown of PNNs promotes juvenile forms of extinction of fear memories in the amygdala
source: Importantly, chemical breakdown of PNNs reactivates ocular dominance plasticity in the adult visual cortex (Pizzorusso et al., 2002), promotes juvenile forms of extinction of fear memories in the amygdala (Gogolla et al., 2009) and functional recovery after brain injury (Bradbury et al., 2002; Gherardini et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PNN degradation and fear memory.

claim: Chemical breakdown of PNNs promotes functional recovery after brain injury
source: Importantly, chemical breakdown of PNNs reactivates ocular dominance plasticity in the adult visual cortex (Pizzorusso et al., 2002), promotes juvenile forms of extinction of fear memories in the amygdala (Gogolla et al., 2009) and functional recovery after brain injury (Bradbury et al., 2002; Gherardini et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PNN degradation and brain injury recovery.

claim: PNNs were proposed to act as a structural brake to experience-dependent plasticity, restricting the extent to which a neural circuit can change during late postnatal development
source: Therefore, PNNs were proposed to act as a structural brake to experience-dependent plasticity, restricting the extent to which a neural circuit can change during late postnatal development (Berardi et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research proposing this hypothesis.

claim: PV cells represent a major subtype of cortical GABAergic interneurons, specialized in providing fast and reliable perisomatic inhibition to principal neurons
source: PV cells represent a major subtype of cortical GABAergic interneurons, specialized in providing fast and reliable perisomatic inhibition to principal neurons (PNs), thereby controlling their output spiking properties and driving network oscillations in the β-γ-frequency range (Freund and Katona, 2007; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cell function.

claim: PV cells control the output spiking properties of principal neurons and drive network oscillations in the β-γ-frequency range
source: PV cells represent a major subtype of cortical GABAergic interneurons, specialized in providing fast and reliable perisomatic inhibition to principal neurons (PNs), thereby controlling their output spiking properties and driving network oscillations in the β-γ-frequency range (Freund and Katona, 2007; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Tremblay et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cell function.

claim: PV cells control cortical circuit activity
source: In addition to controlling cortical circuit activity (Hensch, 2005; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012), PV cells shape sensory plasticity (Fagiolini et al., 2004; Hensch, 2005; Donato et al., 2013; Toyoizumi et al., 2013; Kuhlman et al., 2013; Gogolla et al., 2014; Lensjø et al., 2017; Takesian et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cell function.

claim: PV cells shape sensory plasticity
source: In addition to controlling cortical circuit activity (Hensch, 2005; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012), PV cells shape sensory plasticity (Fagiolini et al., 2004; Hensch, 2005; Donato et al., 2013; Toyoizumi et al., 2013; Kuhlman et al., 2013; Gogolla et al., 2014; Lensjø et al., 2017; Takesian et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cells and plasticity.

claim: The strength of inhibition from PV cells was proposed to define the temporal window of the CP of cortical plasticity
source: In particular, the strength of inhibition from PV cells was proposed to define the temporal window of the CP of cortical plasticity: increasing GABAergic neurotransmission accelerates the onset of the CP, whereas a reduction of inhibition delays the onset of plasticity (Fagiolini et al., 2004; Hensch, 2005; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cell inhibition and critical period timing.

claim: Increasing GABAergic neurotransmission accelerates the onset of the CP
source: In particular, the strength of inhibition from PV cells was proposed to define the temporal window of the CP of cortical plasticity: increasing GABAergic neurotransmission accelerates the onset of the CP, whereas a reduction of inhibition delays the onset of plasticity (Fagiolini et al., 2004; Hensch, 2005; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on GABAergic transmission and critical period timing.

claim: A reduction of inhibition delays the onset of plasticity
source: In particular, the strength of inhibition from PV cells was proposed to define the temporal window of the CP of cortical plasticity: increasing GABAergic neurotransmission accelerates the onset of the CP, whereas a reduction of inhibition delays the onset of plasticity (Fagiolini et al., 2004; Hensch, 2005; Hensch and Fagiolini, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on inhibition and critical period timing.

claim: Very little is known about how PNN accumulation around PV cells changes the cellular and synaptic properties of these interneurons
source: Despite the mechanisms underlying the CP have been extensively studied (Hensch, 2005; Hübener and Bonhoeffer, 2014), very little is known about how PNN accumulation around PV cells changes the cellular and synaptic properties of these interneurons, thus affecting cortical circuits and limiting plasticity.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: Dysfunctions of cortical circuits involving PV cells as well as PNN maturation are implicated in several psychiatric diseases including autism and schizophrenia
source: Indeed, accumulating evidence indicates that dysfunctions of cortical circuits involving PV cells as well as PNN maturation are implicated in several psychiatric diseases including autism and schizophrenia (Marín, 2012; Sorg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cells, PNNs, and psychiatric diseases.

claim: PNN removal in adult mice altered the gain of visual processing in vivo
source: Here, we describe how PNN removal in adult mice altered the gain of visual processing and the power of γ-oscillations in vivo; we reveal the underlying synaptic circuitry and its sensitivity to sensory plasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PNN removal in adult mice altered the power of γ-oscillations in vivo
source: Here, we describe how PNN removal in adult mice altered the gain of visual processing and the power of γ-oscillations in vivo; we reveal the underlying synaptic circuitry and its sensitivity to sensory plasticity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PNNs set the strength of thalamic inputs to PV cells selectively, leaving neuronal excitability and unitary synaptic GABAergic transmission from these interneurons intact
source: In particular, we found that PNNs set the strength of thalamic inputs to PV cells selectively, leaving neuronal excitability and unitary synaptic GABAergic transmission from these interneurons intact.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Selective modulation of thalamic input onto PV cells resulted in a strong and differential modulation of feed-forward inhibition onto PNs and other PV cells
source: This resulted in a strong and differential modulation of feed-forward inhibition onto PNs and other PV cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Plasticity induced by short monocular deprivation (MD) strongly attenuated the effects of PNN removal
source: Importantly, plasticity induced by short monocular deprivation (MD) strongly attenuated these effects, indicating that PNN-mediated modulation of thalamic input onto PV cells depends on visual activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing control and MD conditions shown in Figures 2, 3, and 4.

claim: PNN-mediated modulation of thalamic input onto PV cells depends on visual activity
source: Importantly, plasticity induced by short monocular deprivation (MD) strongly attenuated these effects, indicating that PNN-mediated modulation of thalamic input onto PV cells depends on visual activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that MD attenuates the effects of PNN removal.

claim: ChABC injection 2–3 days prior to electrophysiological experiments effectively and locally disrupts PNNs
source: To test the effects of in vivo PNN removal on adult cortical circuit function, we stereotaxically injected the primary visual cortex (V1) of adult mice (>P70) with the bacterial enzyme chondroitinase ABC (ChABC), 2–3 days prior to electrophysiological experiments (see Materials and methods). This is a standard procedure to effectively and locally disrupt PNNs, revealed by the absence of Wisteria floribunda agglutinin staining (WFA, Figure 1A,B) (Pizzorusso et al., 2002; Lensjø et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing absence of WFA staining in Figure 1A,B and citations to previous research using this method.

claim: ChABC treatment re-opens adult cortical plasticity
source: Importantly, this approach was shown to re-open adult cortical plasticity (Pizzorusso et al., 2002;de Vivo et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gain adaptation of contrast perception is a fundamental computation performed by the primary visual cortex
source: We first measured gain adaptation of contrast perception, which is a fundamental computation performed by the primary visual cortex (Carandini and Ferster, 1997; Anderson et al., 2000; Atallah et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on contrast adaptation.

claim: ChABC-injected animals showed an enhancement of adaptation, measured as a significant decrease of the slope of the transfer function
source: We found an enhancement of adaptation in ChABC-injected animals, measured as a significant decrease of the slope of the transfer function (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The spectral power of the local field potential during both resting state and visual activity was increased by ChABC treatment in the high γ-frequency band (40–80 Hz)
source: Moreover, the spectral power of the local field potential during both resting state and visual activity was increased by ChABC treatment in the high γ-frequency band (40–80 Hz; Figure 1F–I) consistent with a previous report (Lensjø et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F–I and a citation to previous research.

claim: PV cells are known to strongly modulate the gain of contrast sensitivity
source: Importantly, PV cells are known to strongly modulate the gain of contrast sensitivity (Atallah et al., 2012), and improve network synchrony during γ-oscillations (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cell function.

claim: PV cells improve network synchrony during γ-oscillations
source: Importantly, PV cells are known to strongly modulate the gain of contrast sensitivity (Atallah et al., 2012), and improve network synchrony during γ-oscillations (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Buzsáki and Wang, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on PV cells and γ-oscillations.

claim: The enzymatic disruption of PNNs results in increased activity of inhibitory interneurons during visual stimulation
source: Therefore, our results suggest that the enzymatic disruption of PNNs results in increased activity of inhibitory interneurons during visual stimulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results on contrast adaptation and γ-oscillations, combined with knowledge about PV cell function.

claim: The vast majority of layer 4 PV cells in the adult is enwrapped by PNNs to some degree
source: Indeed, we found that the vast majority of layer 4 PV cells in the adult is enwrapped by PNNs to some degree (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C), although in superficial and deep cortical layers (layer 2/3, deep layer 5 and layer 6) the amount of PNNs is much lower (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: In superficial and deep cortical layers (layer 2/3, deep layer 5 and layer 6) the amount of PNNs is much lower than in layer 4
source: Indeed, we found that the vast majority of layer 4 PV cells in the adult is enwrapped by PNNs to some degree (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C), although in superficial and deep cortical layers (layer 2/3, deep layer 5 and layer 6) the amount of PNNs is much lower (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: The probability of recording from PNN-free PV cells in layer 4 of sham-treated animals is very low
source: We conclude that the probability of recording from PNN-free PV cells in layer 4 of sham-treated animals is very low.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that most layer 4 PV cells are enwrapped by PNNs.

claim: Action potential waveform, firing dynamics and passive membrane properties of both PV cells and PNs were unaffected by PNN digestion, in the presence and absence of MD
source: Interestingly, action potential waveform, firing dynamics and passive membrane properties of both PV cells and PNs were unaffected by PNN digestion, in the presence and absence of MD (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Tables S1-2 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and 3, and Tables S1-2.

claim: Previous studies showed altered firing after acute PNN disruption in vitro
source: These results are in contrast with previous studies showing altered firing after acute PNN disruption in vitro (Dityatev et al., 2007; Balmer, 2016), or when the PNN protein brevican was knocked out (Favuzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Previous studies showed altered firing when the PNN protein brevican was knocked out
source: These results are in contrast with previous studies showing altered firing after acute PNN disruption in vitro (Dityatev et al., 2007; Balmer, 2016), or when the PNN protein brevican was knocked out (Favuzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Enzymatic disruption of PNNs significantly increased amplitude and frequency of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) onto PV cells
source: We then analyzed glutamatergic synaptic transmission on PV cells and PNs. Enzymatic disruption of PNNs significantly increased amplitude and frequency of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) onto PV cells (Figure 2A,B; Table S3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B and Table S3.

claim: Glutamatergic transmission onto PNs was unaffected by ChABC treatment
source: Conversely, glutamatergic transmission onto PNs was unaffected by ChABC treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 4; Table S3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4 and Table S3.

claim: Increased neurotransmission onto PV cells following PNN removal was due to quantal synaptic transmission, and not increased slice excitability
source: Increased neurotransmission onto PV cells following PNN removal was due to quantal synaptic transmission, and not increased slice excitability as revealed by increased miniature (m)EPSC frequency in the presence of 1 µM tetrodotoxin (TTX; Figure 2C,D; Table S3 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing increased mEPSC frequency in the presence of TTX, shown in Figure 2C,D and Table S3.

claim: Plasticity induced by MD significantly counteracted the strong increase of sEPSC amplitude and mEPSC frequency on PV cells in PNN-depleted mice
source: Plasticity induced by MD (Pizzorusso et al., 2002; Berardi et al., 2004; de Vivo et al., 2013) significantly counteracted the strong increase of sEPSC amplitude and mEPSC frequency on PV cells in PNN-depleted mice (Figure 2E–H; Table S3 in Supplementary file 1; for ChABC-mediated effects on sEPSC amplitude and mEPSC frequency: p < 0.01 in control vs. p > 0.05 in MD), although sEPSC frequency remained potentiated.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E–H and Table S3, with statistical comparisons.

claim: The increased synaptic recruitment of PV cells, induced by PNN degradation, is sensitive to visual input
source: These results indicate that the increased synaptic recruitment of PV cells, induced by PNN degradation, is sensitive to visual input.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that MD attenuates the effects of PNN removal on glutamatergic transmission.

claim: Changes in the strength of thalamocortical connections were proposed to underlie visual cortical plasticity
source: Moreover, changes in the strength of thalamocortical connections were proposed to underlie visual cortical plasticity (Coleman et al., 2010; Jaepel et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on thalamocortical plasticity.

claim: PV cells exhibited larger light-evoked monosynaptic thalamocortical responses in the absence of PNNs than in control mice
source: In the absence of PNNs, PV cells exhibited larger light-evoked monosynaptic thalamocortical responses (in the presence of TTX and the K+ channel blocker 4-aminopyridine, 4-AP; see Materials and Methods) than in control mice (Figure 2K, Table S4 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K and Table S4.

claim: Plasticity induced by MD significantly attenuated the potentiated recruitment of PV cells by thalamic afferents in the absence of PNNs
source: Importantly, plasticity induced by MD significantly attenuated the potentiated recruitment of PV cells by thalamic afferents in the absence of PNNs (Figure 2L; Table S4 in Supplementary file 1; size effect Glass' delta: 2.11 vs. 1.75; control vs. MD, respectively, see Materials and Methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2L and Table S4, with effect size calculations.

claim: PNN digestion did not affect monosynaptic thalamocortical recruitment of PNs, both in the absence and presence of MD
source: Similarly to spontaneous glutamatergic neurotransmission, PNN digestion did not affect monosynaptic thalamocortical recruitment of PNs, both in the absence and presence of MD (Figure 2M,N; Table S4 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2M,N and Table S4.

claim: AAVs can produce anterograde infection
source: AAVs can produce anterograde infection (Zingg et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: mCherry- (and thus ChR2-) positive cell bodies were never detected in the neocortex in the authors' experiments
source: However, in our hands, we never detected mCherry- (and thus ChR2-) positive cell bodies in the neocortex (Figure 2—figure supplement 6C,D), thus excluding a possible contamination of intracortical responses in our experiments.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6C,D.

claim: PNN accumulation controls the strength of thalamic glutamatergic synapses onto PV cells selectively
source: These results indicate that PNN accumulation controls the strength of thalamic glutamatergic synapses onto PV cells selectively, and this is forcibly modulated by visual activity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on thalamocortical responses.

claim: The strength of thalamic glutamatergic synapses onto PV cells is forcibly modulated by visual activity
source: These results indicate that PNN accumulation controls the strength of thalamic glutamatergic synapses onto PV cells selectively, and this is forcibly modulated by visual activity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing MD effects.

claim: Cortical plasticity is strongly modulated by inhibition
source: Cortical plasticity is strongly modulated by inhibition (Fagiolini et al., 2004; Hensch, 2005; Toyoizumi et al., 2013; Kuhlman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on inhibition and plasticity.

claim: Removal of PNNs is consistent with a more strongly inhibited cortical network
source: Accordingly, we found that removal of PNNs is consistent with a more strongly inhibited cortical network (Figure 1) (Sohal et al., 2009; Cardin et al., 2009; Atallah et al., 2012), and enhanced recruitment of PV cells (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 1 and citations to previous research.

claim: sIPSC amplitude and frequency onto PV cells were increased upon removal of PNNs
source: We found that sIPSC amplitude and frequency onto PV cells were increased upon removal of PNNs (Figure 3A,B; Table S5 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B and Table S5.

claim: AP-independent quantal mIPSC transmission was not affected by PNN removal
source: Interestingly, however, AP-independent quantal mIPSC transmission was not affected by PNN removal (Figure 3C,D; Table S5 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D and Table S5.

claim: Spontaneous GABAergic transmission onto PV cells was due to a network effect, rather than a direct synaptic alteration
source: These results indicate that spontaneous GABAergic transmission onto PV cells was due to a network effect, rather than a direct synaptic alteration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased sIPSCs but not mIPSCs.

claim: Plasticity induced by sensory deprivation prevented the ChABC-mediated increase of sIPSC amplitudes
source: Plasticity induced by sensory deprivation prevented the ChABC-mediated increase of sIPSC amplitudes, whereas frequency was still increased in PNN-depleted mice (Figure 3E–H; Table S5 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–H and Table S5.

claim: sIPSC frequency was still increased in PNN-depleted mice after MD
source: Plasticity induced by sensory deprivation prevented the ChABC-mediated increase of sIPSC amplitudes, whereas frequency was still increased in PNN-depleted mice (Figure 3E–H; Table S5 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E–H and Table S5.

claim: No change in sIPSCs in PNs was found following ChABC injection, both in the absence and presence of MD
source: Importantly, we did not find any change in sIPSCs in PNs following ChABC injection, both in the absence and presence of MD (Figure 2—figure supplement 4E–H; Table S5 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E–H and Table S5.

claim: PNN disruption did not alter unitary GABAergic transmission from PV cells onto themselves, other PV cells and PNs, in terms of magnitude and short-term plasticity, both in the absence and presence of MD
source: Overall, we found that PNN disruption did not alter unitary GABAergic transmission from PV cells onto themselves, other PV cells and PNs, in terms of magnitude and short-term plasticity, both in the absence and presence of MD (Figure 3I–T; Table S6 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I–T and Table S6.

claim: GABAergic synapses from PV cells onto PNs and other PV cells are not altered by PNN removal in the adult mouse visual cortex
source: Altogether, these results indicate that GABAergic synapses from PV cells onto PNs and other PV cells are not altered by PNN removal in the adult mouse visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on unitary GABAergic transmission.

claim: Increased GABAergic spontaneous activity results from increased AP-dependent activity of interneurons
source: Rather, increased GABAergic spontaneous activity results from increased AP-dependent activity of interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased sIPSCs but not mIPSCs or unitary IPSCs.

claim: Thalamic activation of PV cells is very potent in neocortical L4
source: Thalamic activation of PV cells is very potent in neocortical L4 (Gabernet et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2006; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Bagnall et al., 2011), generating strong feed-forward inhibition (FFI), which is responsible for sharpening contrast sensitivity and controlling the temporal resolution of sensory integration (Gabernet et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on thalamocortical activation of PV cells.

claim: Thalamic activation of PV cells generates strong feed-forward inhibition (FFI), which is responsible for sharpening contrast sensitivity and controlling the temporal resolution of sensory integration
source: Thalamic activation of PV cells is very potent in neocortical L4 (Gabernet et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2006; Cruikshank et al., 2010; Bagnall et al., 2011), generating strong feed-forward inhibition (FFI), which is responsible for sharpening contrast sensitivity and controlling the temporal resolution of sensory integration (Gabernet et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research on feed-forward inhibition.

claim: ChABC treatment strongly increased FFI in PV cells, elicited by threshold stimulations
source: We found that ChABC treatment strongly increased FFI in PV cells, elicited by threshold stimulations. Again, MD strongly attenuated this effect (Figure 4A,B, shaded area; size effect Glass' delta: 6.89 vs. 2.30; control vs. MD, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B with effect size calculations.

claim: MD strongly attenuated the increase of FFI in PV cells induced by ChABC treatment
source: We found that ChABC treatment strongly increased FFI in PV cells, elicited by threshold stimulations. Again, MD strongly attenuated this effect (Figure 4A,B, shaded area; size effect Glass' delta: 6.89 vs. 2.30; control vs. MD, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B with effect size calculations.

claim: No change of FFI on PNs was detected when measured at threshold
source: Surprisingly, we did not detect any change of FFI on PNs, when measured at threshold (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: At a higher stimulus intensity (1.5 x threshold), FFI was significantly increased by ChABC treatment also in PNs
source: Importantly, however, at a higher stimulus intensity (1.5 x threshold), FFI was significantly increased by ChABC treatment also in PNs, and sensory deprivation prevented FFI potentiation onto PNs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Sensory deprivation prevented FFI potentiation onto PNs at 1.5 x threshold stimulation
source: Importantly, however, at a higher stimulus intensity (1.5 x threshold), FFI was significantly increased by ChABC treatment also in PNs, and sensory deprivation prevented FFI potentiation onto PNs (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: Compared to PNs, FFI on PV cells was more sensitive to modulation by PNN accumulation
source: Altogether, these results indicate a preferential gating of disynaptic, feed-forward inhibition in L4. Indeed, compared to PNs, FFI on PV cells was more sensitive to modulation by PNN accumulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing differential effects on FFI at threshold stimulation.

claim: The boost of FFI was strongly dependent on visual input
source: In addition, the boost of FFI was strongly dependent on visual input, similarly to s-, m-EPSCs and thalamocortical glutamatergic activation of PV cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing MD effects on FFI.

claim: PNN accumulation in the visual system co-occurs with the end of the CP (P30-35)
source: PNN accumulation in the visual system co-occurs with the end of the CP (P30-35) (Pizzorusso et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research on PNN development.

claim: PNN disruption in V1 of adult mice re-opens cortical plasticity
source: Importantly, PNN disruption in V1 of adult mice re-opens cortical plasticity (Pizzorusso et al., 2002), and is associated to increased glutamatergic synaptic transmission selectively in PV cells (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research and the authors' own data in Figure 2.

claim: The maturation of cortical circuits after the CP is accompanied by a decrease of glutamatergic neurotransmission onto PV cells (both sEPSC amplitudes and frequency)
source: Interestingly, we found that the maturation of cortical circuits after the CP is accompanied by a decrease of glutamatergic neurotransmission onto PV cells (both sEPSC amplitudes and frequency; Figure 5A–C, Table S8 in Supplementary file 1), whereas GABAergic inhibition on PV cells was unchanged throughout development (Figure 5D–F, Table S8 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C and Table S8.

claim: GABAergic inhibition on PV cells was unchanged throughout development
source: Interestingly, we found that the maturation of cortical circuits after the CP is accompanied by a decrease of glutamatergic neurotransmission onto PV cells (both sEPSC amplitudes and frequency; Figure 5A–C, Table S8 in Supplementary file 1), whereas GABAergic inhibition on PV cells was unchanged throughout development (Figure 5D–F, Table S8 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–F and Table S8.

claim: The developmental decrease of glutamatergic strength was selective for PV cells, as both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurotransmissions on PNs were stable across pre- and post-CP stages
source: This developmental decrease of glutamatergic strength was selective for PV cells, as both glutamatergic and GABAergic neurotransmissions on PNs were stable across pre- and post-CP stages (Figure 5G–L, Table S8 in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G–L and Table S8.

claim: The accumulation of PNNs around PV cells during post-CP development determines a change in the excitation-to-inhibition ratio in this interneuron type
source: These results suggest that the accumulation of PNNs around PV cells during post-CP development determines a change in the excitation-to-inhibition ratio in this interneuron type, and ChABC-mediated disruption of PNNs in adult animals (Figure 2) recapitulates some juvenile features of visual cortical circuits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the developmental data showing selective changes in glutamatergic transmission onto PV cells.

claim: ChABC-mediated disruption of PNNs in adult animals recapitulates some juvenile features of visual cortical circuits
source: These results suggest that the accumulation of PNNs around PV cells during post-CP development determines a change in the excitation-to-inhibition ratio in this interneuron type, and ChABC-mediated disruption of PNNs in adult animals (Figure 2) recapitulates some juvenile features of visual cortical circuits.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the effects of PNN removal in adults with developmental changes.

claim: Increased thalamic recruitment of PV cells in the absence of PNNs strongly affects FFI differentially in PV cells and PNs
source: This is associated to a selective increase of thalamic glutamatergic recruitment of PV interneurons in the absence of PNNs, without altering their excitability and the quantal properties of their GABAergic synapses. Increased thalamic recruitment of PV cells in the absence of PNNs strongly affects FFI differentially in PV cells and PNs (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All effects of PNN removal depended on the presence of normal visual input after ChABC in vivo treatment
source: All effects depended on the presence of normal visual input after ChABC in vivo treatment, as they were reduced or prevented by sensory plasticity induced by MD (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Selective decrease of glutamatergic neurotransmission onto PV cells is present during the post-CP development, which is paralleled by accumulation of PNNs around these interneurons
source: Interestingly, selective decrease of glutamatergic neurotransmission onto PV cells is present during the post-CP development, which is paralleled by accumulation of PNNs around these interneurons.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the developmental findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: ChABC degrades chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs), the major PNN component, down to their disaccharide building blocks
source: ChABC degrades chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans (CSPGs), the major PNN component, down to their disaccharide building blocks.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ChABC enzyme activity.

claim: CSPGs are also diffusely present in the entire extracellular environment
source: However, CSPGs are also diffusely present in the entire extracellular environment.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about extracellular matrix composition.

claim: ChABC disrupts the entire extracellular matrix beyond PNNs
source: Thus, ChABC disrupts the entire extracellular matrix beyond PNNs, possibly leading to compounding effects on PV cell circuits, unrelated to PNNs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from knowledge about ChABC activity and CSPG distribution.

claim: The effects reported in the manuscript are due to PNN accumulation around PV cells
source: We thus conclude that the effects that we report in the manuscript are due to PNN accumulation around these interneurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the selective effects observed in PV cells but not PNs.

claim: Genetic ablation of aggrecan (and thus PNN structure) in adult mice results in the re-opening of cortical plasticity
source: Accordingly, it has been recently demonstrated that genetic ablation of aggrecan (and thus PNN structure) in adult mice results in the re-opening of cortical plasticity (Rowlands et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Reduced gain of contrast sensitivity and increased power of γ-oscillations are consistent with increased activity of PV interneurons
source: Reduced gain of contrast sensitivity and increased power of γ-oscillations are consistent with increased activity of PV interneurons.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about PV cell function and the authors' experimental results.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PV cells has a strong effect on the gain of visual contrast sensitivity
source: Indeed, optogenetic activation of PV cells was shown to have a strong effect on the gain of visual contrast sensitivity (Atallah et al., 2012), and determine the level of γ-power and information transfer in the neocortex (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PV cells determines the level of γ-power and information transfer in the neocortex
source: Indeed, optogenetic activation of PV cells was shown to have a strong effect on the gain of visual contrast sensitivity (Atallah et al., 2012), and determine the level of γ-power and information transfer in the neocortex (Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It has been suggested that removal of PNNs in the adult results in alterations of AP waveform and firing
source: Indeed, it has been suggested that removal of PNNs in the adult results in alterations of AP waveform and firing (Dityatev et al., 2007; Balmer, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intrinsic excitability of PV cells and PNs is not affected by in vivo enzymatic digestion of PNNs in the adult visual cortex
source: In contrast, here we show that intrinsic excitability of PV cells and PNs is not affected by in vivo enzymatic digestion of PNNs in the adult visual cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data.

claim: Acute in vitro digestion of PNNs might not entirely recapitulate the actual remodeling of cortical networks induced by visual input
source: Indeed, acute in vitro digestion of PNNs might not entirely recapitulate the actual remodeling of cortical networks induced by visual input.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about methodological differences.

claim: Genetic downregulation of brevican could be prone to developmental and/or homeostatic processes
source: In addition, genetic downregulation of brevican (Favuzzi et al., 2017), a key component of the extracellular matrix, could be prone to developmental and/or homeostatic processes that we did not induce here, due to the relatively short depletion of PNNs in adult animals, known to re-open visual plasticity in adult animals (Pizzorusso et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about methodological differences, supported by citations.

claim: The enzymatic disruption of PNNs is advantageous, because it relies on an acute degradation (2–3 days) at a mature developmental stage when cortical circuits are fully developed
source: The enzymatic disruption of PNNs is advantageous, because it relies on an acute degradation (2–3 days) at a mature developmental stage when cortical circuits are fully developed.
evidence: The claim is the authors' reasoning about their methodological approach.

claim: Compensatory effects are minimal during such a short time of PNN degradation
source: Compensatory effects are minimal during such a short time of PNN degradation, thus allowing dissecting the exact mechanism underlying the re-opening of cortical plasticity, without other developmental effects present when PNNs are removed genetically (Favuzzi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is the authors' reasoning about their methodological approach, supported by a citation.

claim: A recent study suggests that reduced cortical GABAergic neurotransmission is responsible for unlocking juvenile plasticity in adult animals
source: A recent study suggest that reduced cortical GABAergic neurotransmission is responsible for unlocking juvenile plasticity in adult animals, although this was not tested directly, but inferred by spiking activity (Lensjø et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Network-induced FFI and AP-dependent spontaneous synaptic inhibitory neurotransmission were enhanced by PNN removal
source: In fact, here we show that network-induced FFI and AP-dependent spontaneous synaptic inhibitory neurotransmission were rather enhanced by PNN removal, although quantal and unitary GABAergic neurotransmission were not affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data.

claim: Quantal and unitary GABAergic neurotransmission were not affected by PNN removal
source: In fact, here we show that network-induced FFI and AP-dependent spontaneous synaptic inhibitory neurotransmission were rather enhanced by PNN removal, although quantal and unitary GABAergic neurotransmission were not affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data.

claim: The enhanced thalamic recruitment of PV cells and the consequent network-driven increase of GABAergic transmission explain the reduction of the gain of contrast adaptation and the enhancement of γ-oscillations measured in vivo
source: The enhanced thalamic recruitment of PV cells and the consequent network-driven increase of GABAergic transmission (Figure 4G–H) explain the reduction of the gain of contrast adaptation and the enhancement of γ-oscillations measured in vivo (Figure 1), as they are both consistent with increased activity of PV cells (Sohal et al., 2009; Cardin et al., 2009; Atallah et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: Increased FFI onto PV cells and PNs was most likely due to a ChABC-mediated effect on PV-cell recruitment and not on unitary GABAergic responses
source: Increased FFI onto PV cells and PNs was most likely due to a ChABC-mediated effect on PV-cell recruitment and not on unitary GABAergic responses, as they were not affected by PNN depletion, as shown in Figure 3.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data.

claim: FFI on PV interneurons was much more sensitive to the presence of PNNs than FFI on PNs
source: Interestingly, FFI on PV interneurons was much more sensitive to the presence of PNNs than FFI on PNs. This well agrees with the PV cell-specific modulation of sIPSCs by PNNs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data comparing FFI effects in PV cells versus PNs.

claim: The stronger sensitivity of FFI onto PV cells could be due to the significantly stronger unitary PV-PV connections, as compared to PV-PN synapses
source: The stronger sensitivity of FFI onto PV cells, could be due to the significantly stronger unitary PV-PV connections, as compared to PV-PN synapses (p < 0.05).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: The preferential PNN-mediated alteration of FFI onto PV cells might favor L4 circuit disinhibition (and thus paradoxical excitation) for visual stimulations at low intensities
source: The preferential PNN-mediated alteration of FFI onto PV cells might favor L4 circuit disinhibition (and thus paradoxical excitation) for visual stimulations at low intensities, whereas FFI on PNs becomes more prominent at stronger visual stimuli, thus reducing the gain of the visual adaptation curve (Figure 1).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data.

claim: PNN-dependent modulation of FFI in L4 might affect spike-timing precision of both PV cells and PNs, and change the integration window during the initial steps of sensory processing
source: Moreover, PNN-dependent modulation of FFI in L4 might affect spike-timing precision of both PV cells and PNs, and change the integration window during the initial steps of sensory processing (Gabernet et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: The increased glutamatergic recruitment of PV cells induced by PNN degradation could result from alterations induced in the pre- or postsynaptic site (or both)
source: The increased glutamatergic recruitment of PV cells induced by PNN degradation could result from alterations induced in the pre- or postsynaptic site (or both).
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms.

claim: The increase of mEPSC frequency but not amplitude on PV cells, induced by PNN degradation, suggests a presynaptic modulation
source: The increase of mEPSC frequency but not amplitude on PV cells, induced by PNN degradation, suggests a presynaptic modulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data on mEPSCs.

claim: 2–3 days of MD are sufficient to slightly downregulate contralateral thalamic input in the binocular cortex
source: A small, albeit significant, reduction of PV-cell and PN recruitment induced by sensory deprivation in adult mice is present also in control conditions (p < 0.05; not shown), suggesting that 2–3 days of MD are sufficient to slightly downregulate contralateral thalamic input in the binocular cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data that is mentioned but not shown.

claim: In the absence of PNNs, MD effects are more pronounced
source: However, in the absence of PNNs, MD effects are more pronounced.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data comparing MD effects in control versus ChABC-treated animals.

claim: The MD-dependent reduction of PV-cell recruitment is likely the mechanism that is responsible for re-opening cortical plasticity following PNN degradation in adult animals
source: Therefore, we conclude that the MD-dependent reduction of PV-cell recruitment is likely the mechanism that is responsible for re-opening cortical plasticity following PNN degradation in adult animals (Pizzorusso et al., 2002; Rowlands et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data and supported by citations.

claim: In young animals during the CP, sensory deprivation reduces the firing rate of PV cells due to a decrease of synaptic excitatory drive onto these interneurons
source: Interestingly, this effect is similar to that occurring in young animals during the CP, in which sensory deprivation reduces the firing rate of PV cells due to a decrease of synaptic excitatory drive onto these interneurons (Kuhlman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Visual cortical plasticity during CP results from overall decreased inhibition
source: Importantly, visual cortical plasticity during CP results from overall decreased inhibition (Hensch, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A decrease of action potential-dependent inhibition (both on PV cells and PNs) is detected when plasticity is induced with MD
source: Accordingly, we also detect a decrease of action potential-dependent inhibition (both on PV cells and PNs), when we induce plasticity with MD.
evidence: The claim is supported by the authors' experimental data.

claim: In order to induce plasticity in the adult, glutamatergic recruitment of PV cells (and consequently their inhibitory activity) has to increase
source: In order to induce plasticity in the adult, however, glutamatergic recruitment of PV cells (and consequently their inhibitory activity) has to increase (as it happens during the CP; Figure 5 and Kuhlman et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data and supported by a citation.

claim: When PNNs are removed, glutamatergic synapses are enhanced, AP-dependent inhibition too, and this boost is subject to sensory-dependent plasticity that was measured as a decreased level of inhibition
source: When PNNs are removed, glutamatergic synapses are enhanced, AP-dependent inhibition too, and this boost is subject to sensory-dependent plasticity that we measured as a decreased level of inhibition.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: PNN accumulation during post-CP development might exert a protective role, selectively dampening thalamic excitation of PV cells (and thus excessive cortical circuit inhibition) at the expense of reducing cortical plasticity
source: We conclude that PNN accumulation during post-CP development might exert a protective role, selectively dampening thalamic excitation of PV cells (and thus excessive cortical circuit inhibition) at the expense of reducing cortical plasticity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion inferred from the experimental data.

claim: Age-dependent reduction of plasticity of thalamic synapses onto PV cells might be instrumental for correct mature sensory representation
source: Age-dependent reduction of plasticity of thalamic synapses onto PV cells might be thus instrumental for correct mature sensory representation.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental findings.

claim: Deficits in PNN formation during development have been associated with brain diseases involving altered sensory perception, such as schizophrenia and autism
source: Accordingly, deficits in PNN formation during development have been associated with brain diseases involving altered sensory perception, such as schizophrenia and autism (Sorg et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous research.
